proposals.title: Check what the finished runs already show before spending more solver time: val histories, per-band val error, rollouts, restarts
proposals.hypothesis: On the one-step val metric, o1.2's online data cannot beat offline. Three reasons. (a) Both see the same trajectories, with the same exposure per effectively independent sample (256 vs 250). (b) o1.1 was 'level with offline at the same epoch'. (c) val 0.0043 sits at 0.8-1.55x of a plausible aliasing floor (0.0028-0.0055). If the finished o1.2 matches offline within noise on val, per band and in rollouts, then the solver's 147 h per run buys nothing measurable.
proposals.mechanism: o1.2 re-integrates the archived trajectories bitwise. It covers 3,281 time units (TU); offline covers 3,500 TU at 0.02 spacing. The m16 increment decorrelates with integral time 0.0096 TU, which gives ~52 effectively independent targets per TU. So o1.2's 195,250x32x7 = 43.7M draws expose each of ~170.8k effective samples ~256 times, while offline exposes each of its 174,993 pairs ~250 times. The 100x denser pairs carry new information only where the field itself decorrelates within 0.02. That is |k| >= 32-64 (theta band e-folds 0.016 / 0.0076 TU), worth at most ~1-2.6x more independent small-scale states, and these are the most aliased, least predictable scales. Separately, theta[::16,::16] is a subsample, not a filter. The 4096^2 increment variance above |k| = 128 (7.25%) folds into the 256^2 target, so the irreducible MSE lies between 0.5x and 1x of 7.25% of persistence: 0.0028-0.0055. val 0.0043 is inside that range.

proposals.title: Tee the online frame stream to disk during the next production run; replay it for restarts and every later run
proposals.hypothesis: Every o1.2-style run re-integrates the same archived trajectories bitwise. Storing the 256^2 frames once (4.3 TB) turns each later run, and each restart, into a trainer-only job at offline speed (0.387 vs 3.1 s/step), with bitwise-identical data.
proposals.mechanism: o1.2's data are deterministic. Segments are a seeded permutation of fixed checkpoints, the solver is deterministic and checked bitwise against the archive, and each frame is float32 irfft2(qh)[::16,::16]/8. The tee is a writer thread that appends every pushed frame (5,001 per segment, about 1 MB/s per rank: 12 x 256 KB per 3.1 s step) and leaves the loop untouched. Replay pushes the stored frames in the same order with the same flush lag (12 per step; the previous call's frames are stored at the next advance()). n_pairs(t) is then identical, so the CPU torch.randint draws and the batches are too. For restarts: today's resume goes back to best.pt and re-integrates every segment from its i_seg. Those segments are already on disk, so the ~1 h START_SEGS refill and the re-run epochs would cost trainer time only. With frame-ring storage (each frame is stored twice today) the host buffer halves to ~69 GB/rank, which makes buffer snapshots cheap too.
proposals.evidence: SQG/o1.2-TrainUViT_m16_tendency.py L8-11, L23-24, L214-215 (advance/coarse), L255-311 (_push/_flush/advance order), L313-315 (sample: host RNG over min(n_pairs, BUF_SIZE)), L321-328 + L331-335 (resume from best.pt, buffer rebuilt by the solver), L339 (bitwise assert). The code never calls torch.use_deterministic_algorithms (L128-135), so two o1.2 runs are not bitwise-reproducible today anyway (inference from the code). Storage: 5,001 x 262,144 B = 1.31 GB per segment; x 3,281 = 4.30 TB (x 3,500 = 4.59 TB). CHANGELOG.md L68-69: the FIFO stores every frame twice (137 -> ~69 GB/rank). Step times 3.1 vs 0.387 s are the user's numbers (handoff L70-72).
proposals.changes_what_is_computed: no (bitwise) -- same data bits; training differs only by the GPU nondeterminism every o1.2 rerun already has

proposals.expected_gain: The generating run saves nothing; it pays for the stream. Each later run on these trajectories (seeds, ablations, L6/L8 tests, o1.3): 168 h -> ~21 h (-147 h wall, -1,029 H200 GPU-h). If lean_u1 does the generating run: 122 h once, then 21 h. Each restart saves the ~1 h refill plus every re-run epoch: 781 x (3.1 - 0.39) s = 35 min per epoch.

The stream is reusable only while the design keeps m = 16 point-subsampling, the same checkpoint pool, and lags that are multiples of 2e-4. The writer must stay asynchronous. If the owners rebuild the archive or change the coarse-graining, the stream is void.

proposals.title: Make precision an ML quantity: measure E[e|x], the only part of the solver error a trained UViT can absorb
proposals.hypothesis: lean32ek's error (8.8e-6 of Delta, random-walk-like) has zero conditional mean given the input, so the learner cannot absorb it. Its only effect is extra loss variance: (8.8e-6 x 0.27)^2 ~ 5.6e-12 per pixel, ~1e-9 of the 0.0043 MSE. lean32's damping-rate error (mechanism A) is a deterministic linear function of x and will be learned 1:1.
proposals.mechanism: For MSE the population minimizer is f*(x) = E[y|x]. With y = y_true + e, f* = E[y_true|x] + E[e|x]. Zero-mean errors average out and add only variance. A conditional-mean error becomes model bias and accumulates in autoregressive rollouts. Back-of-envelope (inference): lean32's k1-2 delta bias is 3.6e-3 of Delta_k1-2, and Delta_k1-2 ~ 3.7% of theta_k1-2 (band C(0.02) = 0.9993). That is 1.3e-4 of theta per 0.02 step. Relaxing over the ~1 TU (50-step) low-k e-fold, it leaves a standing ~0.7% offset in the k <= 2 amplitude of a plain-f32-trained model; lean32ek leaves none. This complements MATH_delta section 9, which showed the error is invisible in the loss (5e-5 relative for lean32). The loss cannot see a learnable bias, so the bias test has to be done directly.
proposals.evidence: SQG/analysis/opt/delta/MATH_delta.md section 5 (sub-ulp rounding bias), section 7 (lean32ek = mixed, random walk, e_frame 13x over 100x steps), section 9 (UViT relative error 0.079 / 0.24, quadrature argument). SQG/polaris/polaris_sqg_notes.md L1323-1326 (decay quantization: deterministic per mode), L1366-1373 (e_Delta by band), L1453-1454 (archived-state rerun still owed). decorrelation_multigrid_summary.json m16.theta bands_C_at_0.02 k1-2 0.9993, bands_efold_time k1-2 1.06.
proposals.changes_what_is_computed: the test: no; the decision it informs (lean32ek targets in production): yes: data distribution (targets differ by ~9e-6 of Delta)
proposals.test: Polaris debug, 1 node, <= 1 h. Start states: 4 archived checkpoints from 4 members, staged from Midway (4 x 0.4 GB); fallback is the delta_7819310 state. 16 pairs per state, 0.02 apart, for lean_u1 (f64, bitwise production), lean32ek and lean32. One state per GPU: 64 x 4,000 x (6.40 + 3.35 + 3.20) ms ~ 14 min per GPU. Per 256^2 mode: signed mean error over pairs, its standard error, and z. Per band: complex least-squares e_k = beta_k x_k + noise, giving the learnable fraction R^2_k and the learnable bias |beta_k x_k| / |Delta_k|; add a binned-by-|x_k| check for nonlinear conditional means. Pre-registered rule: lean32ek is invisible to the learner if, in every band with >= 1% of Delta's energy, its learnable bias is < 1e-3 of the trained model's own per-band error (from L1) and <= 1% of modes have |z| > 3 (0.27% by chance). proposals.title: Trainer throughput without changing the math: torch.compile the ConvNeXt glue and checkpoint activations for batch 32 on A100 (channels_last is a slowdown)
proposals.hypothesis: About 47% of the UViT's GPU time is fusible glue spread over 3,562 launches per step: elementwise 19.8%, LayerNorm 15.3%, copies 5.2%, memcpy 3.8%, reduce 3.1%. Inductor fusion under strict fp32 should give 1.2-1.4x (estimate, UNVERIFIED). Activation checkpointing restores batch 32 on the 40 GB A100 with no math change.
proposals.mechanism: There are ~1,012 direct_copy kernels per step: circular F.pad before every 3x3/7x7 conv, plus NCHW<->NHWC permutes around LayerNorm/MLP. LayerNorm GammaBetaBackward over few channels is the single largest kernel (8.3%). Compile fuses the pad, permute, LN, GELU-clamp, LayerScale and DropPath chains. GEMM (26.4%) and the native depthwise conv (19.2%) stay. channels_last was measured at +38.5% step time, i.e. 38.5% slower, all of it in backward. The brief's '+38.5%' is that slowdown, not a gain.
proposals.evidence: SQG/polaris/polaris_sqg_notes.md L282-285 (batch 32 OOM, 20.24 GiB at batch 16), L287-303 (416 ms; channels_last 576 ms = +38.5%), L329-353 (kernel families, 3,562 launches), L370 + L411 (channels_last refuted, 'do not adopt'), L395-399 (compile gate: DESIGN section 4.1 compiled-path tolerance <= 1e-2), L450-452 (activation checkpointing gate <= 1e-5). proposals.title: Measure the gradient noise scale at existing checkpoints to decide whether more GPUs can mean fewer, larger steps
proposals.hypothesis: If the gradient noise scale B_simple at mid/late training is well above the global batch 224, the run can use 2-4x the global batch with 2-4x fewer steps at nearly the same number of samples. Wall-clock then drops 2-4x with 2-4x the GPUs.
proposals.mechanism: McCandlish et al. 2018: steps S ~ S_min(1 + B_noise/B) and samples E ~ E_min(1 + B/B_noise), with B_simple = tr(Sigma)/|G|^2. In o1.2's replicated layout every rank keeps its own solver. Doubling the ranks and halving the steps therefore leaves total trajectory time (3,281 TU), fresh pairs per rank-step (12) and reuse (2.7x) unchanged. Only the global batch and the step count change. DDP over CXI costs ~5 ms/step, so replication itself is free.
proposals.evidence: SQG/polaris/polaris_sqg_notes.md L1073-1075 (DDP ~5 ms/step; replicate 4.897 vs 4.887 s on 1 GPU), L896-899 (replication grows the global batch, which changes the recipe). o1.2 L96 (batch 32/GPU), L230-231 (steps per epoch), L408-410 (AdamW + OneCycle).
proposals.changes_what_is_computed: yes: model/training (global batch, LR, step count)
proposals.test: Eval-only on the science machine, 1 GPU, < 30 min. At the offline (or o1.2) checkpoints from an early epoch, a mid epoch and the final epoch: draw 64 independent minibatches of b = 32 training pairs and compute per-minibatch gradients at fixed weights (model.train() for DropPath parity, no optimizer step). Estimate tr(Sigma) from their spread and |G|^2 = |mean g|^2 - tr(Sigma)/(64 x 32); then B_simple. Falsifier: B_simple(late) < 448, meaning no batch scaling. If >= ~900, confirm with one compressed A/B on stored data (global 448, half the steps, LR x sqrt2) before any production change.
proposals.expected_gain: If B_simple >= ~4 x 224: online replicated on 14 H200 goes from 168 h to ~84 h wall at roughly equal GPU-h (~1,176). With lean_u1, 122 -> ~61 h. Offline / replay: 21 h -> ~10.5 h on 14 GPUs. This gains wall-clock only, not GPU-hours.

proposals.mechanism: Online cost scales linearly with steps, because every ML step carries 480 solver steps: T = 168 h x steps/195,250. o1.1's flat val at epochs 50-69 does not show that the remaining epochs are wasted. So the test must compress the whole schedule, not truncate it.

proposals.title: Measure the data-efficiency curve on stored frames: trajectory time (S) vs pair density (STRIDE), and the compute-optimal solver:trainer split
proposals.hypothesis: Val is insensitive to trajectory time between ~1,750 and 3,281 TU (o1.1 matched offline at equal epochs). Then S = 240 (6 fresh pairs/step, 5.4x reuse) gives the same model at half the solver time. Pair density matters only through o1.2's buffer schedule, not in itself.
proposals.mechanism: S and STRIDE are different knobs. S sets trajectory time per ML step, hence the trajectory time covered, hence the independent large-scale states (~1 per 2 TU) and small-scale samples (~52 per TU): the expensive part. STRIDE sets the within-window density. Neighbours 2e-4 apart have 1 - C = 2.7e-3 for targets and 1e-4 for inputs, so they are near-duplicates. In o1.2's code STRIDE 400 also forces S/STRIDE = 1 fresh pair per step, a 1,964-pair start buffer, and a buffer that never evicts, so early pairs are sampled ~150x. Changing S has none of those confounds, which likely explains the reported STRIDE-400 overfit. By the effective-sample count, STRIDE 400 and STRIDE 40 expose each effective sample a similar ~300x vs ~256x. With dval/dTU and dval/dsteps measured, the GPU budget (87% solver today) can be shifted to whichever has the higher marginal return.
proposals.evidence: CHANGELOG.md L339-346 (STRIDE 400 mechanics; proposed discriminator 'STRIDE 40 with every 10th pair buffered'), L453-467. decorrelation_multigrid_summary.json m16.incr.small_lag_fit one_minus_C_at_2e-4 0.0027, m16.theta 1.0e-4. o1.2 L16-22, L184-186. UNVERIFIED: o1.1's S and step count.
proposals.test: Needs stored frames: L2's stream (exact), or as an approximation the dense AllTrainData archive at 0.0025 spacing (extent UNVERIFIED). Emulate o1.2's FIFO exactly (262,144-pair buffer, 4-segment start, uniform sampling) at a 1/4 compressed schedule, with 5 arms: fresh pairs/step in {12, 6, 3} at full density; {12 pairs/step, every 10th pair buffered} (the STRIDE-400 density at STRIDE-40 cost); and {1 pair/step, every 10th pair}, which reproduces the STRIDE-400 schedule. 5 x 5.25 h on 7 H200; score on the L1 scorecard. Falsifier for halving S: the 6-pair arm is worse than the 12-pair arm by > 2x the late-epoch val std, by > 10% in any band, or in rollout low-k energy.
proposals.expected_gain: S 480 -> 240: 168 -> 94.5 h (-73.5 h, -515 H200 GPU-h); lean_u1 122 -> 71.6 h; lean32ek 74 -> 47.5 h. In a decoupled layout it halves the simulators per trainer (lean32ek on A100: ~3.9 -> ~1.9).
proposals.risk: A compressed schedule may reorder the arms. Emulation on the 0.0025-spaced archive is not the 2e-4 stream. Halving trajectory time may matter for rollouts even if not for val. Without L2's stream this test costs online prices.

The 4096^2 increment variance at |k| > 128 is 7.25% (multigrid m1.incr.bandvar), which bounds an aliasing floor at 0.0028-0.0055 MSE.
If o1.1 ran o1.2's 250-epoch OneCycle (UNVERIFIED), its 'flat val at epochs 50-69' happened at 91-97% of peak LR (4.85e-4 to 4.54e-4). That is not evidence that the anneal epochs are wasted.

Forcing (SQG/fixed_ring/A-SQG_data.py L100-105, L342-378): a fixed Hermitian ring of 24 signed modes, |k|^2 in {9, 10, 13, 16} (recounted on the integer lattice), unit amplitude, random phases from jax key SEED_FORCING = 1 (L156). It is added inside the AB3 tendency (L395-403). rms(f0) = sqrt(24), so its direct contribution to the 0.02 delta is ~0.012 in o1.2 units, 4.6% of rms(Delta).

Symmetry: the unforced SQG step (isotropic nu k^2 + mu/k^2 damping, circular 2/3 truncation) is equivariant under grid translations, 90-degree rotations, and reflections combined with theta -> -theta (the Jacobian flips sign under improper maps). With the forcing, a group element preserves F only if the 12 random phases satisfy ~10 extra relations. That has probability zero for continuous random phases (the actual phase draw was not computed here). So no exact augmentation exists for the fixed-forcing system, which agrees with CHANGELOG L345.

The UViT (SQG/model_UViT.py) uses circular padding (L175-177) and periodic RoPE (L87-116). It is translation-equivariant only for shifts that are multiples of 64 coarse cells (5 stride-2 downsamples plus to_vec stride 2), and it is not rotation-equivariant.

The vendored SQG/fixed_ring/A-SQG_data.py is scheme C (DT_SAVE 0.0025 L143, T_PROD 1100 L142) and defines no RUN_CHECKPOINT_DIR, which o1.2 uses at L220. Production o1.2 therefore imports a different (v1) file at ASQG_PY (o1.2 L77), and o1.2's LAG assertion (L182, L187) needs DT_SAVE = 0.02. This matches CHANGELOG L69-70.

o1.2 always resumes from <RUN_TAG>_best.pt (L321-325). It re-runs every epoch after the best one and rebuilds a START_SEGS = 4 segment buffer with the solver (~1 h; L21-22, L331-335). Each re-run epoch costs ~781 x 3.1 s = 40 min online.
The host FIFO stores every frame twice, as y and later as x (o1.2 L291-292; CHANGELOG L68-69).
A tee'd m16 stream needs 5,001 frames x 256 KB = 1.31 GB per segment: 4.30 TB for 3,281 segments, 4.59 TB for all 3,500.
o1.2 runs on GPUs 1-7 of the H200 box (SQG/o1.2-TrainUViT_m16_tendency.sh L9-10).

Concurrency limit (notes L255-268): a threaded solver hides <= 21% of the ML step, and the network's GPU time stretches 4.6x (416 -> 1,910 ms) because the solver alone keeps the GPU 99% busy. MPS (separate processes on one GPU) has no idle resource to use either, so it is not proposed; the expected gain is <= the measured -1.4% (thread_ref).

Projections T = 21 + 147/s (A100 speed ratios; UNVERIFIED on H200): production 168 h; lean_u1 122 h; round 2 f64 ~106 h; mixed 96 h; lean32ek 74 h; lean32ek + trigger + 3-slot ring (estimate) ~64 h. Halving the steps halves T; halving S gives 21 + 147/(2s).

Decoupled sizing with lean32ek on A100: ~1.62 s of solver per 12 pairs / 0.419 s per trainer step = ~3.9 simulators per trainer (notes L890-894 give lean32 3.7). Decoupling leaves GPU-hours unchanged (notes L896-897, L1077-1079).

proposals.title: Polaris 1-node debug 'delta v2': split aliased from resolved error, add a time-step ladder, time lean32ek's fast form
proposals.hypothesis: (a) Most of lean32ek's k=1-2 delta error (2.2e-5) is f32 error in small 4096^2 scales (k>=128) that the subsample folds into the coarse frame. Its alias-free large-scale error should be <=5e-6. (b) Production's own AB3 time error in the 0.02 delta is <=1e-6, about the f64ic32 floor. A dt of 2e-4/30 gives a delta error below lean32ek's precision error. (c) lean32ek + cos trigger + 3-slot ring is bitwise equal to lean32ek and runs at about 2.7 ms.
proposals.mechanism: coarse() = theta[::16,::16], so 256^2 mode k receives every 4096^2 mode k+256m. f32 FFT noise is roughly white in k. It is largest relative to the tendency at k>=512 (4.8e-5 to 1.4e-4 per step, MATH_delta s7), so through the white alias floor it reaches every coarse band. AB3's per-step amplitude error for a mode advected at speed U is about (3/8)(U k dt)^4. NO CHEAP PRECISION CURE PAST lean32ek: (1) compensated products don't help, since product rounding (6e-8 per element) is below the FFT noise (~u*sqrt(log2 N^2) ~3e-7 of the array norm). (2) A lagged f64 correction doesn't help, because FFT rounding decorrelates every step. (3) f64 FFTs with f32 products costs about what lean_u1 does, since FFTs are 66% of lean_u1 (Part X: 3 IRFFT 47% + 2 RFFT 19%). (4) Doing the |k|<=32 part of the product in f64 on a small grid (97.7% of theta variance; ||theta_S||/||theta|| ~0.15) cuts the noise only ~3-5x, to e_delta ~2-3e-6. That costs ~3 extra f32 iFFTs (~+0.5 ms, +15%) and still misses the 1e-6 gate.
proposals.evidence: Sources: MATH_delta.md s11 flags (a) as an untested inference. delta_fidelity.log lines 13-16 (1-step errors) and 26-29 (band e_delta). lean32ek's e_frame is 3.8e-7 at lag 40, which is between the random-walk and coherent accumulation of its per-step error: 3.3e-5 (all-band increment error) x 8.4e-4 (|i|/|theta|) = 2.8e-8 per step, mostly from high k. The multigrid summary (computed here) shows 2.1% of the archive's coarse k1-2 delta variance is aliased. In the synthetic state the k1-2 share of delta is 6x smaller (0.007% vs 0.04%), so its aliased fraction is larger (inference). Notes Part XI table: lean32ek+trigger+ring ~2.7 ms, untested. AB3 numbers computed here with stdlib: imaginary-axis limit 0.7236. At y=0.42: 1.1%/step damping and 1.05% phase error, vs viscous nu*kmax^2*dt = 0.19%/step. At u_rms 8.35 and k_max, y = 0.057, giving 4e-6/step.
proposals.test: Where: Polaris 1-node debug, ~30 min. Run delta_fidelity.py --state-in on the saved 7819310 npz ($MEMBER_ROOT/sqg_profile/delta_7819310/), 8 pairs x 4,000 steps, with new arms: (i) each frame also alias-free (theta-hat truncated to |kx|,|ky|<128, then a 256^2 irfft) plus the alias remainder, with e_delta per band for both; (ii) lean32ek_u1_ring3, checked bitwise vs lean32ek at 40/480/4,000 steps, plus ms/step; (iii) lean_u1 at dt = 2e-4/30, 2e-4/32 and 2e-4/80, with decay recomputed per dt and variable-step AB3 coefficients for the 2 steps after the switch. Richardson estimate of production's time error: e(5e-6) ~ (8/7)|F_5e-6 - F_2.5e-6|. Pre-register the falsifiers: (a) fails if lean32ek's alias-free k1-2 e_delta >= 1e-5; (b) fails if production's time error >= 5e-6, or if the dt/30 e_delta >= lean32ek's; (c) fails if the fast form is not bitwise or is > 2.9 ms.
proposals.expected_gain: Enabler. If (a) and (c) hold, the case for lean32ek's fast form is much stronger: T = 21 + 147/3.44 = 64 h vs lean_u1's 21 + 147/1.45 = 122 h. That is -58 h, or -406 GPU-h on 7 H200s (A100 ratios assumed). If (b) holds, it supplies the evidence for N4 (another 1.33x). (saving x p)/cost ~ 58 x 0.3 / 1 ~ 17.
proposals.risk: The synthetic start state is not archive-like (rms(delta) 0.825 vs 0.27), so aliased shares differ. A dt switch on a saved AB3 history causes a 2-step transient unless variable-step coefficients are used. The debug queue allows one job per user.

proposals.title: Calibrate on Hopper and decompose the 147 h before projecting any speed-up (o1.2 log + Midway H100 NVL)
proposals.hypothesis: Three linked claims. (1) H200 production is ~4.5 ms per solver step, not the bandwidth-scaled 3.0 ms. (2) Hopper's f64/f32 ratio stays ~2-2.5x, so its cheap FP64 doesn't change the precision trade-off. (3) ~0.5 s of the 3.1 s optimizer step (~30 h of the 7 days) is not steady-state solver: buffer fills, epochs re-run after resuming from best.pt, and contention.
proposals.mechanism: The solver is DRAM-bound. On A100 the AB3 fusion runs at SM 6% / FP64 pipe 6%, and the busiest cuFFT kernel at FP64 26%. H200's FP64 gain (~3.5x A100 vector) is matched by its bandwidth gain (3.1x), so FP64 throughput never binds and f32 wins by bytes (~2x plus over-fetch effects). L2 is 50 MB on both H100 NVL and H200. o1.2 always resumes from best.pt, re-runs every epoch after it, and refills 4 segments (800k steps).
proposals.evidence: Notes Part VI job F table (SM 6%, FP64 6%, DRAM 88%). o1.2 lines 21-28 and 88: the 4-segment fill takes '~1 h', i.e. 800,000 steps / 3,600 s ~ 4.5 ms/step on H200. UNVERIFIED: the docstring figure is approximate. User numbers: (3.1 - 0.39) s / 480 = 5.65 ms per solver step including overheads. A100 ref is 9.29 ms; 9.29 x 1.555/4.8 = 3.0 ms bandwidth-scaled (inference). The 1.15 ms/step gap x 93.7M steps ~ 30 h. CHANGELOG: an earlier estimate was 142 h total, not 168 h.
proposals.test: (a) Zero GPU: parse the 7-day o1.2 stdout for the 'buffer filled ... in X s', 'resuming from', per-epoch 's/step' and 'checkpoint loads' lines. Split the 168 h into steady-state solver, fills, re-run epochs and validation. (b) Midway pedramh-gpu H100 NVL, 1 GPU, ~45 min: profile_solver.py plus the seed1/seed2/lean32_precise benches (ref, lean_u1, lean64, mixed, lean32ek, lean32ek_u1_ring3, lean32_u1_ring3); o1.2's serial pattern at batch 32 (fits in 94 GB); ncu dram% on the AB3 fusion and the FFT column passes. Falsifiers: H100 lean_u1/lean32ek ratio > 3 (FP64 or L2 effects would matter), or (a) finds < 5 h of non-solver overhead.
proposals.expected_gain: Value of information. Every projection T = 21 + 147/s assumes the 147 h is all solver and that A100 ratios hold. If ~30 h is overhead, it can be recovered without touching the numerics, and the solver term is ~117 h. For lean32ek's fast form that gives T ~ 21 + 30 + 117/3.44 ~ 85 h (64 h only after the overhead is also fixed). (saving x p)/cost ~ 30 x 0.5 / 1 = 15.
proposals.risk: pedramh-gpu nodes were held by Weidong's no-time-limit generator job (CHANGELOG, In progress). H100 NVL is not H200 (3.9 vs 4.8 TB/s), and Midway's Hopper H100 nodes vary by node class.

proposals.title: Measure how much of the UViT's val error is the irreducible subsample-aliasing floor
proposals.hypothesis: About 0.0020 of o1.1's 0.0043 val MSE (~47%) is the aliased k>=128 content of the target y, which no generator, precision or data volume can reduce. Solver errors at 4096^2 k>=128 therefore matter only through the floor's statistics (its level and shape), not pair by pair.
proposals.mechanism: The 256^2 delta spectrum exceeds the 4096^2 one by a white (5-11)e-7 x Var(delta) per mode. Summed over 65,536 modes that is 0.052 of Var(delta) aliased. For |k|>=128, C(0.02) ~ 1e-4, so delta_alias = y_alias - x_alias with equal variances. x_alias is in the input. y_alias cannot be predicted: a pointwise subsample never sees sub-grid structure at the advected departure points (displacement per 0.02 is ~one 256^2 cell, CHANGELOG 11-02).
proposals.evidence: Computed from decorrelation_multigrid_summary.json (m1 vs m16 incr bandvar). The excess is +3.4e-2 at k64-128 (16.7% of that coarse band), 5.1e-3 at k32-64, and 8.7e-6 at k1-2 (2.1% of the band). In o1.2 units: Var(delta) = (2.2118/8)^2 = 0.0764; aliased delta variance 0.0040; Var(y_alias) = 0.00187 x (8.3493/8)^2 = 0.0020. The CHANGELOG 2026-11-02 entry compared 7.3% vs 5.6% of persistence ('consistent with a floor, not proof'). It ignored that half of delta_alias is x_alias, and its follow-up (per-band val error) was never run. This is an upper bound: SQG fronts may make part of y_alias predictable (inference).
proposals.test: Where: Midway, ~1-2 node-h; needs the user for access to the archive and an o1.1/o1.2 best.pt. Take 1,000-2,000 pairs of 4096^2 theta (t, t+0.02): val trajectories' full fields if stored, else archive frames. Build y_sub (o1.2's coarse) and y_LP (truncation to |kx|,|ky|<128, then a 256^2 irfft); y_alias = y_sub - y_LP. Run the frozen UViT. Report MSE, MSE vs y_LP, Var(y_alias), the fraction Cov(r, -y_alias)/Var(y_alias) of the residual r = pred - y_sub, and the residual spectrum per coarse band vs the white floor. Falsifiers: Var(y_alias) < 15% of MSE, or the model predicts > 50% of y_alias.
proposals.expected_gain: Indirect but potentially the largest lever. If the floor is >= 40% of val MSE, only ~0.0023 is reducible. That frames whether 147 h of solver (1,029 GPU-h) per run is buying anything over offline (o1.1 was 'level with offline'). It also sets the tolerance for every generator change: a 1% shift in 4096^2 k=128-512 variance moves the floor by ~2e-5 (0.5% of val MSE). (saving x p)/cost ~ 147 x 0.2 / 2 ~ 15.
proposals.risk: Val full fields or checkpoints may not be accessible. o1.2's final val may differ from o1.1's 0.0043. Fronts may make y_alias partly predictable.

proposals.title: Larger fixed dt (30 steps per 2e-4 frame) with a per-window CFL guard (adaptive n per window as a variant)
proposals.hypothesis: AB3's margin at the archive's sampled CFL maximum of 0.42 (stability limit 0.7236; the solver aborts at 0.72, warns at 0.60) allows dt = 2e-4/30 = 6.667e-6 (CFL <= 0.56). The 256^2 delta statistics would be indistinguishable from dt 5e-6.
proposals.mechanism: AB3 error per step is ~(3/8)(U k dt)^4. For typical modes (u_rms 8.35, k<=512) that is <= 1.5e-6 at 5e-6, and 3.16x that at 6.667e-6: far below viscous damping (nu*kmax^2*dt = 2.5e-3). Only front cores at k >~ 500 see AB3 damping comparable to viscosity. Any integer n keeps frames on 2e-4 multiples (dt = 2e-4/n). The guard: the step already forms u, v in physical space, so one max-reduction per 40-step window gives umax; a window with CFL > 0.6 is redone at n = 40. Larger-stability schemes don't help: RK4 gives 0.707 per tendency evaluation and SSPRK3 0.577, vs AB3's 0.724. IF/ETD don't address an advective CFL (computed here).
proposals.evidence: A-SQG_data.py lines 133-134 (dt 1e-5 reached a sampled CFL of 0.71; 5e-6 stayed <= 0.42); lines 158-159 (warn/abort); lines 902 and 1016 (CFL = umax*KMAX*DT, KMAX = N/3). At CFL 0.42, umax = 61.5. Delta spin-up CFL ranged 0.315-0.453 (synthetic, max/mean ~1.18), so adaptive n at a 0.5 target would be ~29-30 typically and ~34 at peaks: ~1.35-1.4x, barely above fixed n = 30. The repo holds no archive umax series. The dense NetCDFs store umax every 0.0025 (A-SQG_data lines 615-618), but they are on Midway.
proposals.test: (1) N1's dt arms: paired e_delta vs dt 5e-6, next to production's own Richardson time error. (2) Midway CPU, minutes: from the dense archive's umax, the distribution of CFL at the new dt over the time units o1.2 uses, giving the guard's fire rate. (3) The N5 protocol on archive segments, including full-grid E(k) at k>500 and the coarse corner-band (k128-183) delta variance. Falsifiers: any N5 statistic beyond its pre-set tolerance, or the guard firing on > 5% of windows.
proposals.expected_gain: 1.333x fewer solver steps. Production only: 21 + 147/1.333 = 131 h (-37 h). On lean_u1: 122 -> 97 h (-25 h, -175 GPU-h). On lean32ek's fast form: 64 -> 53 h (-11 h). (saving x p)/cost ~ 25 x 0.4 / 1 = 10 (incremental to N1/N5).
proposals.risk: Frames stop matching the archive bitwise, so o1.2's first-segment assert (lines 336-339) must be replaced. Higher AB3 damping at fronts alters the dissipation range, which feeds the alias floor. Each dt needs its own decay table, plus a 2-step variable-coefficient start.

proposals.title: Statistical-equivalence protocol over o1.2's own 1-time-unit segment horizon, paired against the archive
proposals.hypothesis: lean32ek's errors are unbiased, so its 256^2 delta statistics over a 1-time-unit segment match the archive within 1% of natural variability. Plain lean32 fails the same test at k<=4, as the positive control proving the test has power.
proposals.mechanism: o1.2 restarts every segment from an archived float64 checkpoint and integrates only SEG_T = 1.0, so a generator error acts for at most 1 time unit. Long-run attractor drift is impossible by construction, and the test needs only that horizon. The archive is bitwise the f64 reference, so the reference costs nothing. The yardstick is the f64ic32 control (the state rounded once to f32: the effect of any perturbation the size of one f32 rounding). Unpaired comparisons are weak, so the power comes from the early paired regime, while trajectories are still close.
proposals.evidence: o1.2 lines 9-11 and 86 (SEG_T = 1.0, segments start at archived checkpoints). Notes Part XI: e_frame grows 13x over 100x the steps for lean32ek (random walk) vs 160x for lean32 (bias). Natural snapshot variability, from decorrelation_multigrid.csv (n = 56 archive windows): delta rms CV 15.4%, theta rms 9.7%, delta band fractions 8-18% for k>=8, corner band k128-183 18%, k1-2 65%. So 32 unpaired segments detect only shifts of about 5% or more. The seed1/seed2 READMEs propose a 'Midway twin run' without a horizon, yardstick, power analysis or downstream metric.
proposals.test: Midway; protocol and tolerances accepted by jesswan/Weidong before the run. 32 segments from dense-archive members 1-4 (8 each; reference frames every 0.0025 and checkpoints every 1.0 are already on disk). Per segment: the variant for 1.0 time unit plus the f64ic32 control. Every 0.0025, on o1.2's 256^2 frames (/8) and 0.02 deltas: delta variance per octave including the corner band (the alias floor); delta skewness, kurtosis and 99.9th percentile; theta band variances; band C(0.0025). Plus full-grid SPE, VIE, eps_nu, eps_mu, P, umax and E(k). Gates: G1 (t<=0.3, paired): |mean difference| <= 1% of the snapshot SD and <= 3x the control's. G2: a frozen trained UViT, paired delta-MSE on variant vs archive pairs at identical times <= 1% of MSE (95% CI). G3 (t>=0.5): two-sample agreement within 2 SE, as a sanity check. Positive control: lean32 must fail G1 at k<=4.
proposals.expected_gain: The gate for lean32ek's fast form: T 122 -> ~64 h (-58 h, -406 GPU-h) if accepted. The same harness, built once, then gates N4 (-11 to -37 h), N6 and round 2. (saving x p)/cost ~ 58 x 0.55 / 4 ~ 8.
proposals.risk: Tolerances are a science choice and must be fixed before any run. Completeness of the dense archive is unverified. Cost estimate: ~32 x (~400 s variant + ~700 s control) on H100 NVL ~ 10 GPU-h; UNVERIFIED H100 speeds.

proposals.title: Multi-fidelity generator: 2048^2 restarted from truncated archive states, sampled at the same 256^2 points
proposals.hypothesis: Run at 2048^2 (k_max 683, dt 1e-5, same nu, mu and frozen forcing), restarted every segment from the archived 4096^2 state truncated to |k|<=682. Its 256^2 delta statistics, including the alias floor, would match the archive within natural variability, at 8.7x lower cost per time unit.
proposals.mechanism: The 256^2 frame sees 4096^2 content only through k<~512. Delta variance above k=512 is 0.06% of the total (k512-1024 6.1e-4, k1024-2048 8e-6), vs the 5.2% alias floor, so errors there move the floor by about 1%. theta[::8,::8] on 2048^2 samples the same physical points as theta[::16,::16] on 4096^2. CFL scales with KMAX, so dt doubles at the same CFL 0.42. FFT cost per step scales as N^2 log N, giving 0.229x per step and 0.115x per time unit. Restarting from true states every time unit means only short-horizon fidelity is needed.
proposals.evidence: Multigrid summary, m1 incr bandvar (above). A-SQG_data line 97: k_max*l_nu = 1.76 at 4096^2, hence 0.88 at 2048^2, below the 1.5 criterion. But the under-resolved dissipation range carries <= 0.06% of Var(delta). Computed cost ratios: 2048^2 8.7x; 1536^2 21.5x (k_max*l_nu 0.66, a closure would act on the 256-512 band that holds 1.07% of Var(delta)); 1024^2 77x (misses 341-512, ~10% of the floor).
proposals.test: Stage 1 (Midway, ~5 node-h): a separate 2048^2 step file (A-SQG_data.py untouched), run from 16 truncated checkpoints for 1 time unit each, with N5's statistics vs the dense archive and the f64ic32 control, plus E(k) for k<=682. Stage 2 (decisive, ~15 node-h): offline-style training on 2048^2 vs 4096^2 pairs from the same segments, 20 epochs, 2 seeds each, val on val_m16.zarr. Falsifiers: corner-band delta variance shifted > 2%, or the val difference exceeding the seed-to-seed spread.
proposals.expected_gain: Full replacement: T = 21 + 147/8.7 = 38 h with production code, or 21 + 147/12.6 = 33 h with lean_u1-type code (-135 h, -945 GPU-h). Pretraining only, with a 4096^2 tail for the last 30% of steps: 21 + 147 x (0.3 + 0.7/8.7) = 77 h (-91 h). A decoupled layout would need ~1/9 the simulator GPUs. (saving x p)/cost ~ 113 x 0.3 / 20 ~ 1.7.
proposals.risk: Spectral pile-up near k_max at k_max*l_nu 0.88 could inflate the floor. SQG is somewhat non-local. Frames no longer follow the archive trajectory, so the bitwise assert must go. Science acceptance is uncertain.

proposals.title: Zero-solver pairs: the existing 0.0025-spaced dense archive as an information-equivalent replacement for 2e-4 online pairs
proposals.hypothesis: o1.2's 2e-4 pairs give at most ~2-4x more effectively distinct targets than the stored 0.02 frames of the same trajectories. Pairs spaced 0.0025 apart from the dense archive capture nearly all of that, at zero solver cost.
proposals.mechanism: Target (0.02 delta) correlation is 0.9973 at 2e-4 (fit), 0.92 at 0.0025, 0.47 at 0.01 and -0.07 at 0.02; inputs are 0.9999 and 0.9972 at the first two. So online neighbours are near-duplicates. o1.2 re-integrates 3,281 time units of the same 3,500-unit archive the offline run uses. endorse.comment: Endorse. It is the cheapest decisive item on either list, and the numerics side makes its parity prediction stronger. The rest is below 1e-4, and the estimates there are at noise level. (2) A second term you did not count: the input x is contaminated by the same folding. It holds 16% of the k64-128 band and 58% of the corner band, so the model cannot cleanly sweep the resolved content forward. The per-mode Wiener penalty is <= 1.7e-3 (1.12e-3 of it at k64-128). It is an upper bound, because a CNN can use the cross-scale phase coherence of fronts. Prediction to pre-register: >= 80% of the val MSE sits at coarse |k| >= 64, and the k64-128 band error cannot go below 1.34e-3. If both hold, the model is at the floor where online data adds samples (your |k| >= 32-64 argument), and online cannot beat offline on val by more than ~0.0004-0.002. Use >= 2,000 val pairs: o1.2 L99 uses N_VAL = 200.

Endorse. Numerics view: o1.2's data are a deterministic function of (checkpoint, solver build), so the tee is exact. (a) Free integrity gain: o1.2 bit-checks only the FIRST segment per rank (L283-287). Every tee'd segment contains its 0.02 frames (every 100th), so all 3,281 segments can be checked against train_m16.zarr offline at zero GPU cost. (b) With a tee, the solver becomes a ONE-TIME cost: 656M steps = 1,029 H200 GPU-h (prod), or ~1,170 A100 GPU-h with lean_u1. That changes my priorities. Generate with bitwise lean_u1 (no sign-off needed). lean32ek, dt (N4) and 2048^2 (N6) then save time only on the generating run, so their sign-off is worth less. The 3,281 segments are embarrassingly parallel, so generation can run on any idle GPU, decoupled from training. (c) Lossless time-predictive float compression of 2e-4-spaced frames (1 - C = 1e-4) might give 1.3-2x (UNVERIFIED). Storage sits on the H200 box's /data, not the near-full Eagle.

challenge.issue: The floor range 0.0028-0.0055 ('0.5x-1x of 7.25% of persistence') is built wrong. Val at '0.8x' of a floor is impossible, which is the tell. Three problems. (1) The 1x end double counts: the model returns x + net(x), so x enters exactly and the irreducible part is Var(y|x), not Var(Delta_HF) = Var(y_HF) + Var(x_HF). (2) The isotropic |k| > 128 share of the 4096^2 field includes the in-square corner (128 <= |k| <= 181), which is resolved on the 256^2 grid, not aliased. (3) It misses the input-contamination term. Corrected: floor = Var(y_alias) 0.0023 + an input-alias Wiener penalty <= 0.0017 (+0.0005 if the resolved corner content is unpredictable). That is 0.0023-0.0039 (0.0045), so val is 1.1-1.9x the floor. Your conclusion (near the floor, online cannot buy much on val) survives, more tightly.

challenge.issue: (1) 'lean32's damping-rate error (mechanism A) ... will be learned 1:1' covers only ~20% of lean32's error. The dominant mechanism B (the f32 state rounding each increment) has a conditional mean that is a sub-ulp sawtooth of (theta_k, i_k). Under round-to-nearest-even it should average to ~0 across states (inference): persistent within one trajectory, not a function a regression on x_k sees. So the '0.7% standing low-k offset' is ~5-10x too high. Mechanism A alone is a 0.12% rate error at k1-2, i.e. ~0.06-0.1% in equilibrium amplitude (inference). (2) That makes lean32 a weak positive control. Use a pure mechanism-A arm instead: lean_u1 with only the decay table rounded to f32. Its beta_k is known in advance from decay_quant.py (e.g. at k ~ 8.4: 2.2e-4 of Delta_k8-16), so the test's power is calibrated. (3) 4 states x 16 pairs 0.02 apart gives ~4 independent x values per k1-2 mode (band C(0.02) = 0.9993). Use >= 16 states from >= 4 members (~0.5 GB each), 4 pairs per state.

new_proposals.title: Alias-denoised training targets: train on y_LP (spectral truncation of theta(t+0.02)) with the subsampled input and the val metric unchanged
new_proposals.hypothesis: ~53% of the model's residual variance (Var(y_alias) = 0.0023 of 0.0043) is aliased small-scale content in the target that x cannot predict. If E[y_alias | x] ~ 0, training on y_LP leaves the MSE minimizer unchanged (E[y_sub|x] = E[y_LP|x]) and removes the target-noise part of the per-sample gradient variance, so the same val on y_sub is reached in fewer steps.
new_proposals.mechanism: E(f - y_sub)^2 = E(f - y_LP)^2 - 2E[(f - y_LP) y_alias] + Var(y_alias). The cross term vanishes iff y_alias is uncorrelated with anything predictable from x, and then the argmin is the same. Per-sample gradient 2 J^T (f - y): y_alias adds zero-mean noise. With B_noise >> B late in training (L5), the steps needed scale ~ B_noise. Online cost: a 256x129 slice of the qh that coarse() already transforms, plus one 256^2 irfft per frame. o1.2 already stores x (bx) and y (by) in separate arrays (L291-292), so by can hold y_LP at no extra host memory. Offline: re-coarse-grain the archive's 4096^2 frames at 0.02 once.
new_proposals.evidence: numerics_9.py on decorrelation_multigrid_summary.json: outside-square HF share of Var(theta) 0.002111, which is 0.0023 in o1.2 units (rms 0.048, 17% of rms Delta). o1.2 L215 (coarse = full 4096^2 irfft2 then [::16, ::16]), L291-292 (bx/by separate). decorrelation.py L8, L11, L47: the 0.02 archive holds full 4096^2 frames (m1 computed from them); dtype/size UNVERIFIED. The tr(Sigma) reduction is UNVERIFIED: it depends on how the Jacobian weights high-k output errors.

new_proposals.test: Stage 1 (eval-only, 1 GPU, < 1 h, on N3's 4096^2 pair set; science machine or Midway): at the offline final and a mid-epoch checkpoint, (a) measure Cov(f - y_LP, y_alias)/Var(y_alias), the fraction of y_alias the model predicts; falsifier > 10% (the minimizer would shift). (b) Take tr(Sigma) and the mean gradient over 64 minibatches with y_sub vs y_LP targets on the same x; falsifier: tr(Sigma) reduction < 20% or mean-gradient cosine < 0.99. Stage 2 (only if 1 passes): 1/4-schedule offline A/B, y_sub vs y_LP targets, 2 seeds, val on y_sub with >= 2,000 pairs, per band, rollouts. Falsifier: the y_LP arm is not better at equal steps by more than the seed spread, or its rollout spectra/low-k energy are worse.

new_proposals.title: Sub-cell offset views: theta[i::16, j::16] of the stored 4096^2 states as zero-solver data diversity
new_proposals.hypothesis: The 256 sampling offsets of each 4096^2 state are different coarse views: the same resolved content shifted by a sub-cell translation, with alias images rotated by exp(2 pi i m.delta/16) relative to it. Random centred offsets turn the 175k archived frames into up to 44.8M distinct pairs (o1.2 draws 43.7M). That matches online's draw-level diversity at zero solver cost and teaches the model alias invariance, which targets the train/val gap (o1.1 val/train 1.3, the STRIDE-400 overfit).
new_proposals.mechanism: This is resampling augmentation, not a symmetry, so it does not contradict CHANGELOG L345 (no exact D4/translation symmetry with the frozen forcing). The dynamics are translation-equivariant except for the fixed forcing at k = 3-4. A centred offset of <= 1/2 coarse cell moves the k = 4 forcing phase by <= 0.049 rad. The forcing is 4.6% of rms(Delta), so the worst-case mis-location MSE is 3.6e-7, ~1e-4 of val. The exact alternative is the sampled forcing as an extra input channel. Online the same costs nothing (coarse() with a per-segment random offset).
new_proposals.evidence: o1.2 L215 (pointwise [::M, ::M] after the full irfft2). decorrelation.py L8 and L11-12 (175k full-grid archive frames; point subsampling as 0-coarse_grain.py). Alias shares from numerics_9.py: k64-128 16%, corner 58%. Forcing share from LEARNING's verified facts (A-SQG_data L342-378); arithmetic in numerics_10.py. o1.2 L1-2 (overfit signature). The size and dtype of the 4096^2 archive (~11 TB if f32) are UNVERIFIED.

Then a 1/4-schedule offline campaign on 7 H200: baseline (0,0) vs 16 offsets, 2 seeds each, val at offset (0,0) on >= 2,000 pairs, per band vs the floor table, train/val gap, rollouts. new_proposals.title: Floor-referenced acceptance yardstick for every non-bitwise change (solver precision, dt, resolution, TF32/compile), pre-set by the owners
new_proposals.hypothesis: The irreducible target noise of the m16 subsample, quantified per band here, is the natural scale for deciding whether a non-bitwise change can matter to the learner. By that scale lean32ek is negligible by ~9 orders in variance, while plain lean32's learnable part (mechanism A) can be measured directly.
new_proposals.mechanism: Three pre-set criteria per band with >= 1% of Delta energy: (i) the paired target-perturbation variance is < 1% of floor_b; (ii) the conditional mean (L3's beta_k fit) is < 1% of the model's reducible error in that band (val_b - floor_b from L1); (iii) the shift in Var(theta_HF) (the floor's own level) over N5's 1-TU segments is < 1%. This replaces 'within 2x of a rounding floor', which no float32 tendency can meet, with a test of whether training could tell the difference. It complements N5's statistics and L3's bias test. new_proposals.title: Alias-free training target y_LP: the same minimizer with about half the late-training label noise (privileged information the simulator already has)
new_proposals.hypothesis: About 48% of the late per-pixel residual (Var(y_alias) = 0.0021 of val 0.0043) is label noise that point subsampling creates and no model can predict. Train on y_LP instead of y_sub: the 4096^2 spectrum truncated to the 256^2 square, then a 256^2 inverse FFT. The population minimizer is unchanged if E[y_alias|x] ~ 0, and late per-sample gradient noise roughly halves. If B_noise >~ B (224), the same val is reached in 1.3-1.8x fewer optimizer steps. Online cost scales with steps.
new_proposals.mechanism: For MSE with the tendency model, net*(x) = E[y|x] - x. With y_sub = y_LP + y_alias and E[y_alias|x] = 0, the minimizer is identical. The loss differs only by the constant Var(y_alias), and the per-sample gradient 2 J^T (f(x) - y) loses its y_alias term. McCandlish: steps ~ S_min(1 + B_noise/B). Removing a 48% noise share gives 1.11x / 1.32x / 1.63x / 1.78x fewer steps at B_noise/B = 0.25 / 1 / 4 / 10. Online, y_LP is free: the solver already holds qh, and a truncated 256^2 irfft is cheaper than coarse()'s full 4096^2 irfft. Offline, it needs a one-time spectral re-coarse-graining of the archive's full 4096^2 frames at 0.02. The input stays x_sub and the val metric stays y_sub, so o1.2's yardstick is untouched. An owners' option beyond this: an alias-free input too (spectral coarse-graining) would also remove the x-side 0.0017, but that changes the problem.

new_proposals.title: Make restarts cheap and faithful: resume from last.pt (best.pt only as a NaN fallback) and rebuild the buffer exactly
new_proposals.hypothesis: o1.2 always resumes from best.pt. Combined with a flat, noisy val (o1.1: ~0.0043 for 20 epochs; N_VAL = 200), each restart re-runs about half the plateau, because the argmin of a flat noisy series is roughly uniform over it. That costs ~40 min per epoch plus a ~1 h refill, and it moves the run away from the uninterrupted one (the LR schedule rewinds, and only 4 fresh segments are buffered). This may be the unexplained ~30 h in N2.
new_proposals.mechanism: last.pt is written every epoch with exactly the fields best.pt has: weights, optimizer, scheduler, step, histories, i_seg, n_pairs. So the switch is one line, resume_path = last_path when its val is finite and <= 1.5x best, else best_path. Each restart also spends ~5 segments with no ML steps (4 refill plus the discarded partial one). The pool is 500 per rank vs 474 needed, so after ~5 restarts the wrap-around reuses segments. With L2's tee, the post-restart buffer can be reloaded exactly (69 GB/rank at I/O speed) instead of refilled with 4 new segments.

answers.question: PS challenge (N1/N4): the dt ladder needs a decay table per dt and variable-step AB3 coefficients. Who writes them? What is the bitwise control? Does the dt = 2.5e-6 arm fit the 1-h budget? Pre-register the minimum detectable time error.
answers.answer:
**Who writes it.** The coding session writes a new file, SQG/analysis/opt/delta/dt_ladder.py (A-SQG_data.py stays untouched). It copies lean_solver.make_advance and takes two run-time inputs:
- h: the AB3 coefficients become (23/12, -16/12, 5/12)·h and tdt = f32(h).
- decay_h: built with A-SQG_data's exact expression (L326-329), with DT replaced by h.

The first 2 steps after the switch use variable-step AB3. The past nodes are t_n, t_n - h1 and t_n - h1 - h2:
- b0 = [h^3/3 + (2h1+h2)h^2/2 + h1(h1+h2)h] / (h1(h1+h2))
- b1 = -[h^3/3 + (h1+h2)h^2/2] / (h1 h2)
- b2 = [h^3/3 + h1 h^2/2] / ((h1+h2) h2)

Step 1 uses (h, h0, h0) and step 2 uses (h, h, h0). I checked these in exact rational arithmetic: they reduce to 23/12, -4/3, 5/12 at uniform h and integrate quadratics exactly. For n = 30, step 1's coefficients are (2.296, -1.926, 0.630)·h.

**Bitwise control.** When h == DT the code takes the uniform branch (floating-point b(h,h,h) need not round to (23/12)h). Its frames must then equal lean_u1 bitwise at lags 40, 400 and 4,000, checked on one pair per GPU. A CPU unit test, test_dt_ladder.py, covers the coefficient identities and the convergence order on a scalar test equation.

**What the analysis found.** Production's step is theta+ = d·(theta + i). The exact integrating-factor solution damps the increment by (1 - d)/(rh) ~ 1 - rh/2, so production has a first-order splitting error of -(rh/2)·i per step (inference). Its size relative to Delta is 2.5e-6 at k = 1, 8.2e-6 at k = 128 and 9.3e-4 at k_max.

AB3's own error, (3/8)(Ukh)^4 per step, is negligible at u_rms. In jet cores at U = umax = 61.5 it is not:

| k | AB3 damping / viscous, h = 5e-6 | AB3 damping / viscous, h = 2e-4/30 |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | 13% | 32% |
| 500 | 84% | 199% |

**Arm design.** Production's time error is bracketed without a full Richardson campaign: e(h0) = D(h)·h0^p/(h^p - h0^p).
- For h = 2e-4/30 that is 3.00·D (first order, p = 1) or 0.73·D (third order, p = 3).
- The half-step arm separates the two: D(2.5e-6)/D(2e-4/30) = -1.50 for p = 1 and -0.64 for p = 3. The n = 32 arm cannot (0.75 vs 0.70).
- So the 2.5e-6 arm stays, but on one pair per GPU: 8,000 steps x 6.4 ms = 51 s per GPU, not 410 s.

**Budget per GPU (A100 ms/step).**

| Item | Time |
|---|---|
| 16 pairs x (lean_u1 + lean32ek) | 624 s |
| 4 pairs x (decay-quantization control, f64ic32, lean32, fast form) | 299 s |
| dt arms 2e-4/30, 2e-4/32, 2.5e-6 on one pair | 91 s |
| Controls (production ref, h = DT path) | 63 s |
| Timing | 25 s |
| **Total** | **18.4 min** |

With JIT and checkpoint loads it is ~25 min of the 60-min limit.

**Minimum detectable error.** The dt arms are deterministic float64 runs from identical states. The h = DT control must give exactly 0, and float64 rounding-order chaos is ~1e-15 relative (inference). So the dt measurement is not noise-limited: any D above ~1e-12 is real.

Pre-registered:
- (i) Per band, D(2.5e-6)/D(2e-4/30) lies in [-1.6, -0.55]. Otherwise production's time error is reported only as a bound.
- (ii) The ratio is about -1.5 at coarse k <= 8, where splitting dominates.

For the bias regression on lean32ek (L3), the minimum detectable bias is 2.8 SE. It assumes the same absolute white noise in archive states (inference), 16 independent states, and the 4 pairs within a state counted once at low k:

| Band | Minimum detectable bias (fraction of Delta_band) |
|---|---|
| k1-2 | 6e-6 |
| k2-4 | 1.3e-6 |
| k8-16 | 2e-7 |

The decay-quantization control's known bias at k1-2 is 7e-4, more than 100x above detection.

answers.question: PS challenge (N3/N11): three different Var(y_alias) values are in circulation (0.00207, 0.0023, 0.0024). Compute the resolved-corner term from the measured spectrum and hand the owners ONE pre-registered floor table.
answers.answer:
**Why the three values differ.** All three rest on the same identity:
- Subsampling conserves variance (m16/m1 rms = 1.0000079).
- So the aliased variance equals the 4096^2 variance outside the [-128,127]^2 square: the |k|>=128 share (2.581e-3 of Var(theta)) minus the in-square corner.
- They differ only in how that corner is split.

Where each went wrong:
- LEARNING (0.00207) assumed white alias. The measured per-mode alias is not white: it rises toward the coarse edge.
- Mine (0.0023) used a single per-mode slope of 3.56 across the 128-256 octave. The spectrum steepens there: the octave-ratio slope is 4.50 from 128-256 to 256-512 and 6.09 above.
- PS (0.0024): the ratio() fit gives a 1D slope E ~ k^-2.56 (per-mode 3.56), but corner_integral then uses k^(1-p) with p = 2.56, i.e. a per-mode slope of 2.56. My lattice model at per-mode 2.5 gives a corner of 3.90e-4 and F1 = 0.00239, which reproduces PS's number.

**Calibration.** The alias model lives on the exact 4096^2 lattice:
- one power law per octave, normalized to the measured m1 octave;
- the solver's KMAX cutoff;
- every mode folded exactly onto the coarse grid.

Two checks against the paired, measured m16 - m1 excess:
- The k64-128 excess (1.226e-3) is reproduced within ±4% by every slope from 2.5 to 5.5. This validates the model.
- The k32-64 excess sets the slope inside 128-256: 4.65 from the archive frames (1.655e-4) and 3.85 from the dense frames (1.791e-4, normalized to their own k128-256 level).

**The table** (o1.2 units, slope 4.25; ranges over 3.85-4.65):

| Coarse band | Resolved S | F1 = alias A | A/(S+A) | F2 = Wiener penalty | F1 + F2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| k<32 | — | 5.8e-5 | <=0.002 | 5.8e-5 | 1.2e-4 |
| k32-64 | 1.49e-2 | 1.94e-4 (1.81-2.07e-4) | 0.013 | 1.90e-4 | 3.8e-4 |
| k64-128 | 6.99e-3 | 1.34e-3 (1.32-1.35e-3) | 0.16 | 9.8e-4 | 2.32e-3 |
| k128-183 (corner) | 6.0e-4 (5.6-6.4e-4) | 6.2e-4 | 0.51 | 3.0e-4 | 9.2e-4 |
| **Total** | | **0.00221 (0.00217-0.00225)** | | **0.00152** | **0.00374 (0.00367-0.00380)** |

- Per-mode alias: 1.8e-8 (k<32), 2.0e-8 (k32-64), 3.5e-8 (k64-128), 4.4e-8 (corner).
- Sampling uncertainty: the 56-window standard error of the |k|>=128 variance is 3.7% (window-to-window CV 27%), and the archive and dense levels differ by 5%.
- So F1 = 0.0022 ± 0.0001 and F = 0.0037 ± 0.0002.
- o1.1's val 0.0043 is 1.15x F (1.13-1.17). About 0.0006 is reducible, and 87% of F sits at coarse |k| >= 64.
- F2 is a linear-Gaussian, per-mode estimate. Per-mode is <= per-band by concavity, which is why LEARNING's per-band 0.0017 is higher. A network that exploits front coherence can beat F2.
- LEARNING's central 0.0038 agrees within 2%.

- Average the stored isotropic spectrum (unit-k shells, written at every theta save) over at least 100 frames.
- Feed P(k) = E(k)/n_shell(k) into numerics_14_lib.py (stdlib, seconds).

answers.question: User's request: what is the specific math behind the lean32 / lean32ek / mixed / floor table?
answers.answer:
**The metric.** e_Delta = ||Delta_v - Delta_ref|| / ||Delta_ref|| = e_frame x ||F|| / ||Delta||. The magnification ||F||/||Delta|| is 1.83 at 4,000 steps in the test state, about 3.9 in archive-like states, and about 25 inside the k1-2 band.

**Row 1, lean32 (all float32).** The float32 state rounds every increment. Per step the error is |rho|/|i| <= u|theta|/|i|, with u = 2^-24. At k1-2 the increment is 9.8e-6 of theta, so the error is 6.1e-3 per step, which reproduces the measured 1-step error of 5.3e-3. Slow modes keep the sign of the sub-ulp remainder for many steps, so the error builds up as a bias, not noise: e_Delta is flat in L at k2-4 (2.0e-3) and 3.6e-3 at k1-2. The float32 decay table is mechanism A (rate error 0.12% at k = 1, -15.7% at k = 8.41) and accounts for about 20% of it.

**Rows 2-3, lean32ek and mixed.** The compensated state (TwoSum and Fast2Sum, roughly a 48-bit state) leaves only the float32 tendency. Its 1-step increment error is 3.29e-5, i.e. 3.29e-5 x 8.44e-4 = 2.8e-8 of theta per step.
- These errors stay partly correlated over ~40 steps: e_frame(40) = 3.8e-7.
- After that they random-walk: e_frame(4000) ~ 3.8e-7 x sqrt(100) x 1.28 (chaotic growth) = 4.8e-6, against 4.82e-6 measured.
- So e_Delta = 4.8e-6 x 1.83 = 8.8e-6.

**New this round: the absolute per-mode spectrum of the coarse delta error.**
- lean32ek is near-white: 7e-16 to 4e-15 per mode (o1.2 units squared), a max/min spread of 5x.
- lean32 is red: 2.4e-12 to 6.3e-10, a spread of 260x.
- So lean32ek's '2.2e-5 at k1-2' is white, aliased FFT noise divided by the tiny k1-2 share of Delta's energy (6.8e-5). It is not a large-scale dynamical error. lean32's error is a slow-mode bias.

**Row 4, the floor (f64ic32).** One float32 rounding of the state (rms 2.5e-8 of theta) gives e_frame = 4.0e-8, which grows to 1.27e-7 over 0.02 time units (3.1x). So e_Delta = 2.3e-7.

**ms/step.** The step is memory-bound.
- lean32: 3.20 ms.
- lean32ek: 3.35 ms. The extra complex64 'lo' array (134 MB per step at 0.90 TB/s) adds 0.149 ms.
- mixed: 4.73 ms. Keeping theta-hat and both tendencies in complex128 adds 1.38 ms.
- Against production's 9.29 ms these are 2.90x, 2.77x and 1.96x.

**What the learner sees.** lean32ek's per-mode error variance (~1e-15) is 1e-7 to 1e-8 of the per-mode alias floor (1.8-4.4e-8). As noise it is invisible. Only a conditional mean could matter, and the Step 2 regression measures that.

answers.question: PS to LEARNING on L1: 0.0043 is a mid-schedule plateau, o1.2 may not have finished, there are three floor tables, and N_VAL = 200 is noisy. What is the fallback, which floor table, and what is the SE?
answers.answer:
(1) What 0.0043 is. My 91-97%-of-peak-LR arithmetic assumed that o1.1 ran o1.2's schedule. That is UNVERIFIED and probably wrong: o1.2 lists 'the SAME number of optimizer steps as offline' as one of its changes from o1.1. One thing does hold. Offline runs the 250-epoch OneCycle, and o1.1 was 'level with offline at the same epoch'. So OFFLINE's val was also about 0.0043 at epochs 50-69, where the LR is 4.85e-4 to 4.54e-4. 0.0043 is therefore a mid-schedule value. Only the final, annealed offline val may be compared with the floor, and STEP 0 retrieves it.

(2) Fallback if o1.2 did not finish. Every epoch E is at the same LR in both runs: both have 781 steps/epoch and total_steps 195,250. Both runs also score the same 200 val pairs (seed 42). The pre-registered comparison is therefore paired by epoch, over the last 10 complete o1.2 epochs E*-9..E*. It reports d = mean_E(v_o1.2[E] - v_off[E]). The SE is the std of the paired d divided by sqrt(10), times sqrt((1+r1)/(1-r1)) to correct for lag-1 autocorrelation r1. The checkpoint-level per-band eval compares o1.2@E* with offline@final. That comparison is one-sided: only 'o1.2 is better' is informative. Offline is re-run to E* (21 h x E*/250) only if the history comparison is ambiguous. If o1.2 finished, compare the final last.pt checkpoints.

(3) One floor table. It supersedes my 0.00207, NUMERICS' 0.0023 and your 0.0024 (see the next answer).

(4) SE of N_VAL = 200. The per-frame CV of the high-k variance is 0.27, of Var(theta) ~0.19 and of Var(Delta) ~0.31 (n = 56 frames). A per-pair loss CV of 0.25-0.40 gives SE(200) = 1.8-2.8% of val (7.6e-5 to 1.2e-4 at 0.0043), and SE(2,000) = 0.56-0.89%. This error is a fixed offset shared by every epoch and by both runs. Because the runs share the pairs, a run-vs-run difference has SE sqrt(2(1-rho)) x SE: 0.6-1.3% at rho = 0.9-0.95 (the losses are floor-dominated). So a 10% band difference is detectable. The largest effect online could possibly have, ~0.0005 or 12%, is 3-6 paired SE: detectable only paired or with >= 2,000 pairs.

STEP 0 formula (it uses the per-trajectory lines and the startup bincount): SE = sqrt(J/(J-1) x sum_j (n_j/n)^2 (v_j - vbar)^2). This is an upper bound if J is small, because real between-trajectory differences inflate it.

answers.question: PS: converge on ONE floor table before the readout, and compute the resolved corner from the archived E(k).
answers.answer:
Method. I fitted an isotropic per-mode spectrum P(k) of the 4096^2 field: a piecewise power law with knots at 2^j and the 2/3 cutoff N/3. I then folded it exactly onto the 256^2 lattice, mapping each fine K to K mod 256, mode by mode over the whole 2/3 disc.

Out-of-sample validation. A fit to the m1 octaves ONLY predicts the measured m16 alias excess and corner band without using them. Archive: k64-128 to 1.2%, corner k128-183 to 2.2%. Dense: 0.4% and 1.1%. k32-64 comes out 0.2-15% high, a small absolute amount. So the aliasing model is confirmed quantitatively.

The resolved in-square corner is 21% of the 4096^2 |K| >= 128 variance: 5.8e-4 of 2.81e-3 in o1.2 units. The spectrum steepens across 128-256 (per-mode slope -4.1 there, -5.3 above), which puts more of that band inside the square than a single-slope fit does. That is why 0.0023 / 0.0024 were slightly high and my white-alias 0.00207 was low.

TABLE (o1.2 units, archive; dense in brackets). Columns: y_alias A = hard floor if E[y_alias|x] = 0 | per-mode Wiener input penalty W | central A+W.
- k < 16: 1.4e-5 | 1.4e-5 | 2.8e-5
- k16-32: 4.4e-5 | 4.4e-5 | 8.8e-5
- k32-64: 1.97e-4 | 1.93e-4 | 3.9e-4
- k64-128: 1.34e-3 | 1.00e-3 | 2.34e-3 (alias share of the band 16%)
- k128-183 (corner): 6.3e-4 | 3.0e-4 | 9.3e-4 (alias share 52%). If the resolved corner is entirely unpredictable, the corner is A + S = 1.22e-3.

TOTALS. lo = Var(y_alias) = 0.00222 [0.00212]; central = 0.00377 [0.00359]; hi (corner unpredictable) = 0.00406 [0.00385]. 86.5% of the central floor sits at coarse |k| >= 64.

Uncertainty. Smoothness variants of the fit move it +-1%. Frame sampling is +-4% (SE of the band means over 56 frames). The archive and dense sources differ by 5%. Combined: about +-5%.

Bounds. lo is a lower bound only if E[y_alias|x] = 0. Central is not a bound in either direction: nonlinear de-aliasing at fronts lowers it, and closure/backscatter unpredictability of the resolved scales raises it.

Pre-registered predictions for the final models:
- P1: >= 80% of val MSE at coarse |k| >= 64.
- P2: per-band error >= 0.9 x A_b in k32-64, k64-128 and the corner.
- P3: on held-out 4096^2 frames, the residual regressed on y_alias has slope -1 +- 0.1 in every band (the model predicts < 10% of y_alias).
- P4: final val >= 0.95 x lo. Otherwise the floor model is refuted.

At val 0.0043, the share reducible by ANY change is 12% (archive) to 17% (dense) against central, and 48-51% against lo. So 'within 1.5x of the floor' holds trivially against central and fails against lo. I propose that the pivot decision key on the DIRECT paired per-band o1.2-vs-offline differences, not on a floor ratio.

answers.question: PS to LEARNING on L3: what MDE do 16 states x 4 pairs give, does it beat the gate, and which positive control calibrates it?
answers.answer:
Sample count. At 16 states x 4 pairs (P = 64), the k1-2 band gives 4 complex modes x 64 = 256 complex samples. x barely changes across a state's 4 pairs (C(0.02) = 0.9993), but lean32ek's noise is independent per pair. SE(beta) depends on sum|x|^2 and the noise, not on the number of independent x. Independent x only matter to separate the intercept from the slope and for the binned nonlinear check.

MDE (|z| = 3, 80% power = 3.84 SE) of a real, band-common beta, in units of |Delta_b|. lean32ek's measured per-band noise is scaled x2.1 to archive states (MATH_delta s3: ||F||/||Delta|| is 3.9 vs 1.83):
- k1-2: 8.0e-6
- k2-4: 8.8e-7
- k4-8: 2.6e-7
- k8-16: 1.2e-7
- k >= 16: ~8e-8

Against my round-1 gate (bias < 1e-3 x the model's per-band relative error eps_b), the test clears lean32ek at k1-2 only if eps_k1-2 >= 0.8% (k2-4: >= 0.09%). Nothing guarantees that, so as written the job could prove nothing.

I replace that gate now, before any run, with a derived one. A learned bias accumulates coherently over the band's memory, n_b = tau_b/0.02 rollout steps: 53, 56, 17, 4.9, 1.8, 1, 1 from the m16 theta e-folds. The model's own random error accumulates as sqrt(n_b). Requiring the bias to stay below 10% of that in amplitude (<= 1% in variance) gives g_b = 0.1/sqrt(n_b) = 0.014, 0.013, 0.024, 0.045, 0.075, 0.1, 0.1. With this gate the test clears lean32ek if eps_model,b >= 5.8e-4 (k1-2), 6.6e-5 (k2-4), 1.1e-5 (k4-8), and <= 2.6e-6 above that. eps_model,b comes from the STEP 1 readout, so STEP 1 must precede STEP 2's pre-registration. - n = 2: -1.5e-4 (z -51)
- n = 9: +2.4e-3
- n = 16: -8.5e-4

answers.question: PS to LEARNING on L5/L6: GRAD_CLIP = 1.0 and AdamW break the McCandlish mapping; the L6 precursor should be a gate.
answers.answer:
L5. Production clips the DDP-averaged global-batch (224) gradient at 1.0 every step. The B_simple estimator uses raw per-minibatch gradients at fixed weights, so clipping does not bias the estimate itself. What clipping and AdamW (beta2 0.95) do break is the mapping from B_simple to how many steps a larger batch saves.

Revised: at each probed checkpoint, report the clip-active fraction: the share of 16 global batches (7 x 32 pairs each) with ||g_224|| > 1.0, plus the norm quantiles. The batch-scaling conclusion is directional only. The only decision-grade evidence is a compressed A/B at global batch 448 on stored data. If clipping is active in most late batches, the effective late-training LR is also below what OneCycle says, which matters for L6's schedule reasoning.

L6. The precursor is now a gate. It uses offline val_loss_history from STEP 0: v125, v200, v249, and sigma_late = std(v240..v249).
- GO for both the 1/2 and the 1/4 arms if v125 - v249 <= max(2 sigma_late, 2% x v249).
- 1/2 arm only if that fails but v200 - v249 <= max(2 sigma_late, 2%).
- Otherwise the last 50 epochs still move val by more than 2%: run the 1/2 arm only, with its prior cut to 0.2.

The gate is one-directional. Mid-LR val carries iterate noise that any anneal, compressed or not, removes. So a large v125 - v249 does not prove the steps are needed; only a small one proves they are not.

answers.answer:
o1.1 used all 3,500 checkpoints at SEG_T = 0.5 (1,750 TU), half of o1.2's buffer, reuse ~10, and a step count different from offline. It was level with offline at equal epochs 50-69.

Reuse 10 at 32 draws per step means 3.2 fresh pairs/step, which is S ~ 128 if STRIDE stayed 40 (UNVERIFIED). Trajectory time consumed by epoch 70 = 70 x 781 x S x 7 x 5e-6 = 245 TU (S = 128), 459 (S = 240) or 918 (S = 480). That is at most 26% of offline's 3,500 TU. At S = 128 o1.1 could not even consume its 1,750 TU within 250 epochs (it would need 500).

So the natural experiment already says this: at mid-schedule (high LR), one-step val is insensitive to trajectory time down to ~250-900 TU, and to 10x reuse vs 50-69 passes. That covers L11's 1,750-vs-3,500 arm and L8's 'halve S' at mid-training, more strongly than either arm would.

What it does not settle:
- the annealed endpoint;
- per-band and rollout metrics;
- confounds from FIFO locality and buffer size.

Pre-registration. STEP 0 extracts o1.1's config (wandb config: s, stride, seg_t, buf_size, n_epoch), its val history, and TU per epoch (o1.2 logs online/time_units; o1.1 is UNVERIFIED). Three cases:

- o1.1 stopped mid-schedule: L11 runs.
- o1.1's final val differs from offline's: L11 runs.
When L11 runs, it adds what o1.1 cannot: an annealed endpoint at a controlled TU; contiguous-vs-striped SEG_T at equal TU (NUMERICS' checkpoint-diversity point); per-band and rollout scoring; and the seed spread from L6's replication pair.

## 1. The math behind the delta-fidelity table (user's question, verified vs `polaris_delta_7819310/delta_fidelity.log` + `MATH_delta.md`)
